contentBlocks.text: Last week you supported an essay claim with Claim-Evidence-Reasoning in writing. Today: the same skill, spoken aloud!

A speech is more convincing when a main point is backed by real evidence, just like a written paragraph — but spoken evidence needs to be brief and memorable, since a listener can't pause and reread a long statistic like a reader could. Pick one of the two main points from your Day 1 outline, and write one short, specific piece of evidence (a fact, example, or brief statistic) to support it in speech.
You just added real evidence to your speech! Tomorrow you'll practice and deliver the whole thing.

objectives: Understand why spoken evidence must be brief and memorable
Write one short piece of evidence supporting a main point from the child's own outline
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review last week's Claim-Evidence-Reasoning essay skill briefly.
2. Explain why spoken evidence needs to be shorter/simpler than written evidence.
3. Have the child write one piece of evidence for one of their Day 1 main points.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's full speech delivery.
differentiationTips: Struggling: offer a concrete example first (e.g. 'I know a lot about basketball because I've played for 5 years') as a model to adapt
Ready for more: ask the child to write evidence for both main points, not just one
Deliberately connects back to last week's written CER skill, showing the child the same reasoning transfers across writing and speaking
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is an open-ended activity — check that the evidence is specific and genuinely brief enough to say aloud in one sentence.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Grade 8 Speaking and Listening standard SL.8.4: presenting claims with relevant evidence, sound reasoning, and well-chosen details.

generationData.instructions: Add spoken evidence to one of your main points.

prompts.prompt: Which main point are you supporting?
